title: Bacolod anti-Pax Silica protest raises alarm over proposed copper mine
summary: More than 200 protesters take to the streets in Bacolod City, linking the proposed Colet Copper mining project in Negros Occidental to the Pax Silica initiative

items: A youth-led protest in Negros Occidental focused on a proposed copper mining project linked to the US-backed Pax Silica initiative, raising concerns about potential exploitation of local mineral resources.
Protesters, including young professionals and students, expressed fears that the initiative could lead to foreign exploitation of natural resources and harm local communities and the environment.
Local officials emphasized the need for any mining company to establish legal rights and coordinate with the Mines and Geosciences Bureau before proceeding with operations in the area.

NEGROS OCCIDENTAL, Philippines – A youth-led protest against a US initiative to secure supplies of critical minerals and advanced technology turned its focus to a proposed copper mining project in southern Negros Occidental, raising questions about the potential exploitation of the province’s mineral resources for the US-backed Pax Silica initiative in Luzon.

More than 200 young professionals and college students gathered at the Paghimud-os (Struggle) Statue at the Capitol Lagoon in Bacolod City on Monday, November 16, linking the proposed Colet Copper Project (CCP) between Hinoba-an and Sipalay City to the Pax Silica initiative.

Florence Guzon, vice president of Kabataan Party-list and spokesperson for Bayan Negros, told the rally that Cooper Metals Ltd was pursuing the copper mining project, which was in the permitting stage.

blocks.caption: What is Pax Silica? What are its goals, and what concerns does it raise?

blocks.text: Documents presented to the media showed that the project would target the Don Jose copper deposit, first identified in the 1960s and subjected to successive exploration and evaluation campaigns from the 1970s to 2012 through a series of joint ventures.
The proposed mining area lies within the South West Negros Mineral District, a 60 x 60-kilometer mineral belt hosting porphyry copper deposits in the Sipalay-Basay-Hinoba-an area.

The project site is about 20 kilometers by road from the coast of Hinoba-an and 25 kilometers from Sipalay, according to the documents, which did not identify the specific barangays covered by the application.
A 2012 Seminco Cooper Study said conventional open-pit mining and flotation operations could recover copper concentrate from the targeted deposit.

Previous operators reportedly completed more than 124,000 meters of drilling, geological mapping, geochemical and geophysical surveys, metallurgical sampling, mine planning, infrastructure engineering and environmental baseline studies.
On Tuesday, November 17, the Environmental Management Bureau-Negros Island Region (EMB-NIR) said the application was subject to evaluation by the Mines and Geosciences Bureau (MGB).

But earlier, EMB-NIR officer-in-charge Vicente Losban̈es said the bureau had no record of Cooper’s reported application, adding that most mining areas in southern Negros Occidental, including Sipalay, Hinoba-an, Candoni and Cauayan, were already titled properties belonging to Philex Mining Corporation and Maricalum Mining Corporation.
Philex explored the area through its Bulawan (Gold) Project in the 1980s and 1990s and operated commercially from 1996 to 2002.
Maricalum began exploring gold deposits in southern Negros in 1955 and started commercial operations two years later. It suffered financial collapse in 1985 and eventually ceased operations in 2001.

“If Cooper wants to enter the mining hubs in southern Negros, it must have consent from either Philex or Maricalum,” Losbañes said. “But we’ll see. We’ll check if they indeed have a pending application now, especially with the Mines and Geosciences Bureau.”

Hinoba-an Mayor Daph Reliquias told Rappler on Tuesday, November 17, that any company seeking to source minerals in southern Negros for Pax Silica should first establish the legal status of the mineral areas and coordinate with the MGB.

“If Pax Silica or an affiliated company intends to expand into Southern Negros and source minerals for its project, it should first establish the legal status of the mineral areas and coordinate with the Mines and Geosciences Bureau (MGB),” Reliquias said.
“Even if Philex has no actual mining operations in Southern Negros at present,” Reliquias said, “its existing mineral agreement or mining tenement may still carry legal rights and obligations.”
Pax Silica is a US initiative aimed at building a secure and stable supply chain for computer microchips amid the expansion of artificial intelligence and other advanced technologies.
Guzon said the reported copper mining application was reason for the youth to remain vigilant.
“We can’t close our eyes now. We will see to it that Pax Silica won’t invade the country, including Negros Occidental, to cull and haul our critical minerals in southern Negros,” he added.

blocks.caption: NUPL seeks release of anti-Pax Silica protesters detained for over 36 hours

blocks.text: The protesters said they feared the initiative could lead to greater foreign exploitation of the country’s natural resources and threaten local communities and the environment.

Breech Pedrajas, a 23-year-old nursing graduate and youth campaigner for the Negrosanon Initiative for Climate and the Environment, said they would continue protesting against Pax Silica when necessary.

“That’s why we oppose its purpose, which comes at the expense of our environment, especially water resources, so, we, the Negros youth, are protesting Pax Silica,” said Pau-Pau Gonzales, 20, an education student at the University of St. La Salle-Bacolod.
Bianca Montilla of Youth for Climate Hope said Pax Silica would bring in US technologies that were unsuitable for the country’s environment and come at the expense of indigenous people.
Rusty Biñas, founder of the Green Alert Network, lauded protesters from various environmental and youth organizations who took to the streets.

“Allowing global supply-chain agendas like Pax Silica to carve open southern Negros for copper extraction would only trade our agricultural resilience and economic self-determination for permanent disaster risk and foreign control,” he said.
“We need only look at the cautionary legacy of Maricalum Mining, which left Sipalay with scarred farmlands and generational ecological hazards instead of genuine development,” Bin̈as stressed.
He said his organization would stand with the youth in defending the province’s land, water and indigenous communities.
Transport and cause-oriented groups also held a separate anti-Pax Silica rally outside the Bacolod Public Plaza on Monday morning. – Rappler.com
